title: Code of Conduct
text:
Community rules:

Be respectful: Treat all participants with respect and kindness. Harassment, discrimination, or any form of abusive behavior will not be tolerated.
Camera and microphone etiquette: When participating in video calls, ensure your camera and microphone are used appropriately. Mute your microphone when not speaking to minimize background noise. We ask that you keep your camera on during sessions to foster a more engaging and interactive environment, but we understand that there may be circumstances where this is not possible.
Stay on topic: Keep discussions relevant to the purpose of the community. Off-topic conversations should be taken to private messages.
Share knowledge: Contribute your expertise and insights to help others. Be open to learning from others as well.
Report issues: If you encounter any problems or witness rule violations, report them to the moderators.

title: Join ReModel
text:
ReModel will run in 2 monthly cycles, with each cycle focusing on a different simulation model. Each cycle will consist of two sessions: a Running session and a Reusing session.
Session 1: Running - this session will be an opportunity to clone and run the model, reproduce an existing result or scenario, and confidently explore the model and its outputs. Participants will be encouraged to ask questions and share their insights.
Session 2: Reusing - this session will focus on the technical aspects of the model, including its structure, implementation, data requirements and input assumptions. Participants will consider what they would change, whether they understand the model well enough to make those changes, and how an edited model should be checked and documented.
Each session will last for 1 hour, and will follow a participative discussion format.
The sessions are free to attend, but spaces will be capped at 15 places per session on a first-come, first-served basis; NHS analysts will receive priority.

title: Join ReModel
text:
Register for ReModel
You can sign up for one, several or all ReModel cycles. Each cycle focuses on one open simulation model and includes two linked sessions: Running and Reusing. Registration for a cycle covers both sessions in that cycle.

Cycle 1: Non-Elective Flow Simulation
Cycle 1 focuses on the open-source Non-Elective Flow Simulation, a discrete-event simulation of patients moving from the emergency department into same-day emergency care or an inpatient bed. We will explore how bed capacity, length of stay and same-day emergency care activity affect queues and waiting times.
Registration for this cycle covers both online sessions and will open on 13 August 2026 and close on 2 October 2026:

Running the model: 11am-12pm - 7 October 2026
Reusing the model: 11am-12pm - 28 October 2026

Sign up for Cycle 1


Cycle 2: Meeting the demand of NHS 111 for primary care services
Cycle 2 focuses on MOOOD, an open-source discrete-event simulation that follows callers after an NHS 111 primary-care disposition and models their subsequent contact with primary care, NHS 111, ambulance services and emergency departments. We will explore how timely primary-care contact affects activity across services and potentially avoidable emergency department attendance.
Registration for this cycle covers both online sessions and will open on [insert date] and close on [insert date]:

Cycle 3: The Value of Triage during Periods of Intense COVID-19 Demand
Cycle 3 focuses on an open R simulation of intensive-care triage during periods of intense COVID-19 demand. We will explore how first-come, first-served admission, demand-based triage and reverse triage interact with demand, length of stay and capacity, and affect lives and life-years lost.

title: Reusing: The Value of Triage during Periods of Intense COVID-19 Demand: Simulation Modeling Study
text:
This open R simulation by Wood and colleagues examines hypothetical intensive-care triage strategies when COVID-19 demand might exceed capacity. It compares first-come, first-served admission, triage when demand is expressed and reverse triage. Inputs include demand, length of stay, capacity and assumptions about patient outcomes; outputs include lives and life-years lost. The model has been independently reproduced through the STARS project.
How to join


All sessions


Cycle 1: Running Non-Elective Flow DES
Cycle 1: Reusing Non-Elective Flow DES
Cycle 2: Running NHS 111 primary care DES
Cycle 2: Reusing NHS 111 primary care DES
Cycle 3: Running triage during intense COVID-19 demand
Cycle 3: Reusing triage during intense COVID-19 demand





This session will consider whether participants understand the model well enough to reuse it. Participants will:

describe how they think the model is structured from patient inputs through to reported outcomes;
compare that understanding with the R scripts and simulation implementation;
identify how arrivals, length of stay, capacity and triage rules are represented;
locate the data and assumptions controlling the supplied scenarios;
discuss what they would change for a different question or use case;
trace a selected input assumption through the code to a published output; and
use the reproduction evidence to identify how a change should be checked, validated and documented.

The aim is for participants to be able to identify an assumption they would change, locate it in the model and assess whether they understand the implementation well enough to make the change confidently.




Retain the working R environment and editable repository from Session 1.
If you did not attend Session 1, confirm that you can complete the selected model run before this session.
Consider one input, rule or scenario you would change and why the change would be analytically useful.

title: Running: Nonelective Flow DES
text:
The Non-Elective Flow Simulation is an open-source discrete-event simulation developed by Helena Robinson at Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Foundation Trust. It represents patients moving from the emergency department into SDEC or an inpatient bed and explores how bed capacity, admitted length of stay and SDEC activity affect queues and waiting times. The model is written in Python using SimPy and includes a Streamlit interface.
How to join

Open the model repository and follow the instructions to get the model running. Participants should aim to: - clone the GitHub repository and identify the files needed to get started; - create the supplied Python environment and install the dependencies; - start the Streamlit application and run the simulation; - reproduce an existing scenario and check that the run has completed as expected; - explore the existing controls and interpret the principal outputs.
Alternatively, participants can use CodeSpaces to explore the model without a local installation (see README for details). The aim is for participants to come to the session with a successful model run that they can continue to explore.

title: Reusing: Meeting the demand of 111 for primary care services
text:
MOOOD is an open-source discrete-event simulation developed by Richard Pilbery and colleagues. It follows callers after an NHS 111 primary-care disposition and represents subsequent contact with primary care, NHS 111, ambulance services and emergency departments. The Python and SimPy model compares the existing system with timely primary-care contact and reports activity across services and avoidable ED attendance.
The original data and parameters relate to callers registered with Bradford and Airedale GP practices, so reuse elsewhere requires local review and validation.

title: ReModel: Read, Run, Reuse
text:
Building a simulation model from scratch is a time-consuming and resource-intensive process. ReModel aims to make it easier for healthcare analysts to read, run, and reuse existing open simulation models. We recognise that within healthcare there is a potential to reuse existing models because many of the problems faced by healthcare systems are similar as are many of the pathways experienced by patients. ReModel is a project that aims to make it easier to read, run, and reuse open simulation models.
Our goal is to empower people within the NHS to:

run open source simulation models on their own machines
critique/assess/evaluate simulation models with their pros and cons
repurpose existing simulation models for their own use cases

This is the website for ReModel - a club for healthcare simulation enthusiasts to meet and engage in reusing open simulation models.
Our mantra when it comes to healthcare simulation is Read, Run, Reuse.
There is already a wealth of simulation models that are not being used to their full potential. ReModel is a project that aims to change this by making it easier to read, run, and reuse open simulation models.
If you are a healthcare analyst with an interest in simulation, or a simulation modeller who wants to learn how to better share your work, then ReModel is for you.
This website is a hub for ReModel activities. ReModel is hosted by the Strategy Unit.
Find out more about taking part and take a look at previous and upcoming sessions.

title: ReModel: Read, Run, Reuse
text:
How we are funded
ReModel has been funded in 25/26 as part of the national Strategic Commissioning Intelligence Centre (SCIC).
Simulation modelling can be effectively used in strategic commissioning by:

Analysing complex systems: It allows organizations to evaluate different scenarios and make data-driven decisions, which is crucial for strategic planning in commissioning.
Identifying resource needs: Simulation modelling helps in understanding the current state of health services and identifying underserved communities, enabling better allocation of resources.
Evaluating service impacts: It allows for the assessment of the impact of various service changes on population health and resource utilization, ensuring that commissioning decisions are evidence-based.
Supporting economic evaluation: By analysing the economic return on investment for interventions, simulation modelling aids in prioritizing services and ensuring that resources are used efficiently.
Facilitating transparency: It promotes transparency in decision-making processes, allowing stakeholders to understand the rationale behind commissioning decisions.
